projects.title: 做了一个不用划词、没有悬浮窗的三指查词， AI 解释这个词在这句话里的意思（Tauri 直出 4 端）
projects.author: laizenan
projects.summary: 大家好，分享一个桌面查词工具。 **一句话**：鼠标指着生词，Mac 三指轻点触控板（ Windows 双击 Ctrl ），面板贴着这个词出现，告诉你它在这句话里是什么意思，旁边是你自己的 MDict 词典。没有悬浮窗，不叫它，它不存在。 官网 / 下载（ 20M 超小体积）： https://aalookup.com 74 秒演示视频（ B 站）： https://www.bilibili.com/video/BV1txeJ6dEz7/ ![]( https://iili.io/nCbq11V.png) ## 为什么又造一个 我读英文的场景很杂：论文 PDF 、各种网页、桌面应用，还有游戏。用过的工具大致两类： - **划词翻译类**：得先选中；很多要常驻一个悬浮球，或者监听选区，一不小心就弹出来；给的是整句翻译，而我要的是「这个词在这里什么意思」。 - **截屏翻译类**：快捷键、框选、OCR 、整块翻译。对付游戏可以，读网页和 PDF 太重，也接不上自己的词典。 我想要的其实是 macOS 自带「三指轻点查词」的手感——指过去、点一下、看完就散——但要在所有 App 、PDF 和游戏里都能用，要解释语境义，要能用我自己的词典，查过的词还得记得住。没找到，就自己写了一个。 ## 它是怎么查词的 **触发**：Mac 三指轻点 / Force Click / 快捷键（默认 ⌃⌥D ）； Windows 双击 Ctrl / 快捷键（默认 Ctrl+Alt+D ）；也可以绑一个鼠标键。不需要先选中任何东西。不想指、想直接打字查，Ctrl+M 呼出一个小搜索框。 **取词**：优先走系统辅助功能接口（ macOS Accessibility / Windows UI Automation ），直接拿到指针下面这个词和它所在的整句。是原文，不是 OCR 猜出来的。只有在选不中文字的地方——游戏、图片、视频字幕——才用本地 OCR （ macOS 走 Vision ，Windows 是本地模型）。 **显示**：面板是非激活窗口（ macOS 上是 NSPanel ，Windows 上 WS_EX_NOACTIVATE ），贴着那个词出现，不抢焦点、不进 Dock 、不进任务栏；原文里的词会有一个系统样式的高亮。点别处就收起。 **内容**：左栏是 AI 流式给出的「在这句话里的意思」和用法、语法，右栏是本地 Mdx/在线词典的词条——原版排版、例句、发音、图片都保留，你用什么词典就是什么词典。AI 拿到的输入是词 + 整句 + 词典文本，所以它做的是「在你的词典里挑对义项并解释」，不是自由发挥。离线或次数用完时，词典栏照常。词典是本地的，面板出来的同时就在； AI 那一栏随后流式补上。 **屏幕模式（实验性）**：⌘⌃A （ Windows Ctrl+Alt+A ）把当前画面冻住，点上面的词查，或框一块区域按 OCR 取词，顺手可以标注、打码、复制、存 PNG 或贴图到最上层。识别都在本机。这是给「整屏都选不中字」的场景准备的，例如 Tooltip 悬浮窗里的字，鼠标过去就没了，选不到。 ## 和你可能在用的工具，差别在哪 | | 划词翻译类 | 截屏翻译类 | AALookup | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | 触发 | 选中 → 弹出 | 快捷键 → 框选 | 指向 → 轻点 | | 取到什么 | 你选中的文字 | 框里的像素 → OCR | 指针下的词 + 它所在的整句（原文） | | 结果 | 整句翻译 | 整块翻译 | 这个词在这句里的意思 + 你的 MDict 词条 | | 平时 | 常见悬浮球 / 监听选区 | 常驻 | 菜单栏一个图标，只听触发手势 | | 游戏 / 图片 | 选不中 | 可以 | 可以（本地 OCR ，按需开） | | 查完之后 | — | — | 生词本 → FSRS 复习 → 手机 / 网页同步 | ## 平时完全静默 - 没有悬浮窗、悬浮球、常驻面板。Mac 上是 Accessory 应用，平时不占 Dock ，只有菜单栏一个图标； Windows 上是托盘图标。 - 不监听选区、剪贴板；只有你设置的触发手势 / 快捷键在听。 - 不上传内容：只有你触发查词、且开着 AI 解释时，才发送这个词、所在上下文（默认约 700 字符）和相关词典文本； OCR 在本机完成，截图不上传。 - 面板收起后，屏幕上不留任何东西。 ## 查完之后 点一下收藏，词连同原句进生词本，FSRS 排复习；内置高考 3500 、CET-4/6 、考研、IELTS 、TOEFL 、GRE 词书，跟写、拼写、听写、默写四步，练过的词进同一个复习队列。登录后桌面、手机（ Android APK / iOS TestFlight ）和网页 https://aalookup.com/learn 同步生词和进度。 ## 词典从哪来 目前还需要自己去你懂得网站上找 mdx 词典； AI 解释不依赖你装了什么词典，但装了词典解释会更准——它会先读你的词条然后总结出最符合上下文的那一条。 ## 价格 本地完全免费。AI 次数会送一点，用完以后回退本地模式。AI 和同步功能按月付，需要高强度使用的时候再开。 ## 想听的反馈 - 作为第 1000 个词典和第 10000 个英语学习工具，还是想了解一下你自己觉得现在使用的工具的痛点在哪里。 - 准备搞一个可以直接下载的词典，你觉得最想要哪种词典？

projects.title: Show HN: Swift-Qwen3.8-27B, -58.3% thinking, x1.95 speed, accuracy of xhigh
projects.author: kisjovan
projects.summary: Hi everybody, we post-trained Qwen 3.8 27B to be more efficient by figuring out which tokens were linked to overthinking and penalizing them without "attacking" the reasoning length directly then fixed the accuracy with a bit of secret sauce (hint On-Policy Distillation) and achieved great results (-58% length, 1.95x speed up, <1% accuracy loss) so we wanted to open-source it and hear the feedback of the community. This is the link to the model: https://huggingface.co/ukisai/Swift-Qwen3.8-27b / It's at 80k downloads in 3 days with independent evals here: https://www.reddit.com/r/LocalLLaMA/comments/1wg7dd5/ukisai_... We are also providing a Free Research Purpose API (OpenAI compatible), courtesy of Nvidia who were kind enough to provide us with the GPUs. It's limited at 5RPM. https://ukisai.com/api/swift/v1/models We also made a GGUF (Q1-Q8): https://huggingface.co/ukisai/Swift-Qwen3.8-27B-GGUF and there's also a few nice community quants with even lower/higher precision (Bartowski: https://huggingface.co/bartowski/ukisai_Swift-Qwen3.8-27b-GG... ). The community also created amazing MLX, NVFP4, W4A16 and Uncensored versions you can find on Huggingface. IMPORTANT: Our training approach is not a replacement for the reasoning effort settings, chat templates or token caps but is complementary and targets a completely separate issue (overthinking and "anxiety-like" reasoning loops prior seen in PTQ, but as far as we identified also prominent in BF16 of this size class LLMs as well). Contrary to popular belief, these specific patterns do not contribute to answer quality when properly targeted. (our thesis being: reasoning length IS extremely important and should NOT be shortened by force, but rather optimized). This is also demonstrated bellow in our xhigh vs medium effort benchmark. The goal is to keep xhigh accuracy while reducing only the unnecessary part of thinking. The TLDR of our thought process, research, training and a link to the Meta paper that inspired us is in the first comment. The benchmarks: Swift-27B vs Qwen3.8-27B (BF16, all benchmarks ran x5, thinking effort xhigh) GPQA-Diamond: 88.4% -> 88.3%, 58% fewer median tokens LiveCodeBench v6: 76.8% -> 81.6% (+4.8pp, due to default truncation in LCB it is not performance gain), 46% fewer median thinking tokens Terminal-Bench 2.1: 66.7% -> 65.8%, 39% fewer median tokens MMLU-Pro: 85.5% -> 85.0%, 28% fewer median tokens C-Eval: 90.0% -> 90.6%, 19% fewer median tokens IFBench: 73.5% -> 71.8%, 51% fewer median tokens AIME 2026: 98.7% -> 94.0%, 50% fewer median tokens HMMT (Nov 2025): 99.3% -> 96.0%, 46% fewer median tokens ERQA (vision): 67.5% -> 66.3%, 55% fewer median tokens Token savings hold at every reasoning effort (mean thinking reduction): xhigh 41%, medium 23%, low 26% (albeit with accuracy loses of 1-4% on medium and 1-2% on low which we need further testing for) Swift at xhigh vs the base's own effort settings on GPQA-Diamond (198 questions x 5 seeds): Base xhigh: 88.4%, 6,642 median tokens Swift xhigh: 88.3%, 2,771 median tokens Base medium: 84.1%, 1,753 median tokens So Swift keeps xhigh accuracy at under half the tokens, and beats base-medium by 4pp at roughly 1.6x its tokens. End note: While we are keen on complete open-source, we still need to keep a part of our training and data private, being a new lab. The license is not Apache 2.0, but it only affects companies >$1M. We hope this does not pose a problem for the community and are open to feedback on it. We want to contribute as much as possible to the community and would really appreciate feedback on our work, quantization or Swift model requests. We are working on Swift 3.8 Flash Next and have so far gotten up to -53% thinking token usage. We have strong indicators our methodology is reproducible on other model families as well and are asking the community which ones you want us to optimize next.

projects.author: tekfen
projects.summary: Hi HN, I’m a software engineer, and for the past several months I’ve been building Remind Cards, a flashcard app I originally made because I wanted a better way to study Estonian vocabulary. https://remindcardsai.com/app What started as a small prototype gradually became a much bigger side project. The app now supports: * AI-generated flashcards from any topic * Uploading photos of handwritten notes and turning them into flashcards * Automatically generating example sentences for your cards * Pronunciation and text-to-speech, so you can hear the words and example sentences * Custom decks and sub-decks * A 7-box Leitner spaced-repetition system * Multiple study modes: multiple choice, typing, matching, writing, and listening * Images for flashcards * CSV import/export * Offline studying * XP, streaks, achievements, and leaderboards Most of the learning functionality works locally. I mainly use the backend for authentication, synchronization, subscriptions, and shared/community features. One thing I deliberately avoided was turning the app into just an “AI wrapper.” AI helps with getting learning material into the app — for example, you can photograph your handwritten notes and generate flashcards from them, or have it create example sentences — but the actual learning experience is based around active recall and spaced repetition. I’ve built the whole thing as a side project alongside my full-time job. The first prototype took only a couple of days, but I’ve now spent hundreds of hours polishing all the small things around it. I’d especially appreciate feedback on: 1. The study/review workflow 2. Whether the app feels too feature-heavy 3. The spaced-repetition approach 4. The handwritten-notes → flashcards work

projects.title: Show HN: Modern RSS reader with social capabilities based on AT Proto
projects.author: fuegoio
projects.summary: Hey HN! The web is a bit broken and looking at social medias like X makes me a bit depressed. I feel like the original content that we had before on a multitude of website has been replaced by ton of click-bait content that just want impressions and reactions. I would like us to go back to simpler times, where everyone had their publishing space (their website, or an hosted solution) and everyone could subscribe to it in their own software and do what they want with their feed. I still think that social is important, like sharing, because afterall it's what made social networks interesting in the first place, but it should happen outside of where the content is. That's why I wanted to build an RSS reader that is respectful of this principle of federation: no in-app reader, just RSS subscriptions. And I've added social capabilities based on the AT Protocol, like sharing / liking and following people. The project was coded with AI, but it's my convictions that I've put it in. It's self-hostable and I hope that more and more people will be convinced to publish on their own website instead of X / Bluesky.

projects.summary: Back Me Up is a tiny science-ish machine that finds published papers that back your argument. It stemmed from a conversation with a friend around life sciences, where we kind of landed at "surely there’s a paper confirming most arguments", i.e. coffee is bad, coffee is great, etc. You enter a claim, e.g. "drinking wine is good for the heart" -> the system does a semantic search across a corpus (PMC, bioRxiv, medRxiv and arXiv) -> pulls in relevant quotes if they fit your claim, and gives you a verdict. Frontend was done with a combination of Sol + Opus, I spent a bit of time exploring different designs and landed on this slightly ridiculous printer that spits out your evidence. Some notes: - I have no accuracy evals, this was a throwaway thing I built, so no clue on reliability. It does pass the vibe test, so give it a whirl! - Initially built a RAG for a tiny set of PMC, but scaling that up seemed like a lot of work for an evening project. Luckily found an API that does the semantic search across the different sources.

projects.title: 开源了一款网页高亮、批注与 AI 理解的 Chrome 插件
projects.author: phoenine
projects.summary: 平时上班摸鱼我都会在浏览器里读一些感兴趣的文章，看到讲得有意思的段落就划一道，有不同想法的时候还想添上一两句批注，比如记下自己踩过的坑，或者对这处结论存疑。最麻烦的是遇到一些不同学科的专业术语。一个没见过的词卡在句子中间，我得开个新标签页去搜，或者打开 ChatGPT 去询问，搜完还要再回来当前的页面。这样操作很繁琐，因为我只是想简单的知道这个术语的含义而已。 所以今年 5 月，我把这两件事做成了一个 Chrome 插件。划线、批注和术语解释都收在同一个地方，要进笔记库的时候，整份导出成 Obsidian 的 Markdown 就行。同时，也让它支持了跨设备同步的功能，换电脑的时候，登录同一个账号，这些内容也能跟过来。 ![771]( https://wechat-2025-1258175280.cos.ap-nanjing.myqcloud.com/images/%E5%BC%80%E6%BA%90%E4%B8%80%E6%AC%BE%E7%BD%91%E9%A1%B5%E9%AB%98%E4%BA%AE%E3%80%81%E6%89%B9%E6%B3%A8%E4%B8%8E%20AI%20%E7%90%86%E8%A7%A3%E7%9A%84%20Chrome%20%E6%8F%92%E4%BB%B6-1789377118060.png) 这款 Chrome 插件叫六彩，目前是 1.0.0 ，基于 MIT 协议，仓库在： https://github.com/phoenine/liucai 有兴趣的小伙伴可以玩玩。

projects.title: Show HN: I made an 8 bit game that teaches beginners to pwn basic C programs
projects.author: udbhavs
projects.summary: I've been hosting small CTF for my alma mater high school every summer for the last few years, usually in the form of a sequence of website-based challenges that students could complete in an hour or two. This year, now that LLMs are startingly more capable (and people claiming CTFs are dead), I wanted to see if I could design challenges in a way that would minimize the ability to "drag and drop" them into a simple chat window and have it be solved for you, and at minimum require some intuition and interaction from the players. Seeing how bad frontier models were at the ARC AGI 3 benchmark (this pre-Astra), I thought it would be fun to translate aspects of pwning a program to spatial game-based mechanics and try to have some of the "reasoning" happen in the game world instead of all in code. This resulted in challenges where they have to interact with code to change parameters in the game to solve puzzles. While players do have to read code, the game expects no prior knowledge of C programming specifically, and tries to explain concepts such as structs, byte hex encoding, null-terminated strings, endianness, etc. from scratch. It has 10 rooms and builds up to the player being made to do a buffer overflow to clear the final room. There are items the player acquires to inspect source code, see program memory, and translate raw bytes to unsigned 4-byte ints or ASCII strings. There are still some gaps in the ramp up that could be better filled in and might require more hand-holding for complete beginners (I am thinking of adding an item that explains basic C semantics such as variables, conditionals, loops, I/O etc. when you directly hover over the code in the computer). Would love feedback from people here!

projects.title: 做了一个浏览器插件：阅读网页时顺手发现成语
projects.author: cobola
projects.summary: 最近做了一个 Chrome 浏览器插件，叫「妙笔」。 它最初的想法很简单：平时看文章、看新闻、看公众号时，经常会遇到一些成语，但看到之后就过去了，很少真正记住。 所以我做了一个“发现成语”的功能。 安装插件后，阅读网页时可以： - 自动识别页面中的成语 - 查看成语解释、出处、例句 - 收藏自己感兴趣的成语 - 记录每天发现了哪些成语 - 发现冷门成语或之前没注意过的表达 - 对文章进行基础文字检查 我比较喜欢的是“发现成语”这个功能。 它不是强行打断阅读，而是在正常浏览网页的过程中，把文章里出现的成语整理出来。看到一个以前没注意过的成语，可以顺手点开看看；如果是第一次发 现，还可以收藏下来，慢慢积累自己的成语库。 目前插件支持 Chrome 浏览器，适合： - 喜欢阅读中文文章的人 - 学生和家长 - 写作、编辑、自媒体从业者 - 想积累成语和表达方式的人 - 平时经常看长文章的人 网站地址： https://miaob.net https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/cgablamblomanjndbiagjmgnlbkfhfpm 插件和词库是开源的,欢迎提交反馈。 http://github.com/cobola/miaob-extension/ https://github.com/cobola/miaob-dictionary 个人觉得它还比较适合亲子阅读。家长和孩子一起读文章时，可以把当天发现的成语整理出来，之后复习一下，不需要专门拿出一段时间背成语。 现在产品还在持续完善中，欢迎大家试用。如果遇到识别错误、解释不准确，或者有其他建议，也可以直接反馈。 为了感谢大家，准备了 50 个“妙笔本月卡”兑换码，先到先得。兑换码需要在网站登录后，在“妙笔本”页面兑换。 兑换码： MIAOB-F733ADF3C7 MIAOB-F543BBA7FF MIAOB-134DA9604B MIAOB-B7DBEDA36E MIAOB-2F06497344 MIAOB-F20350883C MIAOB-FC1B870232 MIAOB-6D7925E0A7 MIAOB-B37776CBBE MIAOB-A5A14E548B MIAOB-30359A93EA MIAOB-3FC7059EF2 MIAOB-7EF690C8C6 MIAOB-EB2960A511 MIAOB-08658A5FF9 MIAOB-FFBD6341B4 MIAOB-A572BE2B74 MIAOB-F79CD41761 MIAOB-DF09BB3B9B MIAOB-48A5917ACD MIAOB-989CAD1941 MIAOB-09EF9E0A50 MIAOB-AC78EA2F11 MIAOB-369F5E10C3 MIAOB-E3FA4EB0B0 MIAOB-F53CDDCB2E MIAOB-D66903EC6E MIAOB-584498345C MIAOB-1A9133006A MIAOB-DD1425C808 MIAOB-E2D12AF4A7 MIAOB-C7073E3C7A MIAOB-38F3F0F145 MIAOB-B25A947E75 MIAOB-B2EC08A85E MIAOB-B847A0AD2E MIAOB-5E6A900A1E MIAOB-901989AEA0 MIAOB-28A3BB3F05 MIAOB-7D4BE2BB62 MIAOB-74C56992A0 MIAOB-D385896D61 MIAOB-41790BF1CD MIAOB-0DE4E0C8D4 MIAOB-BBBE490259 MIAOB-FF1DF9118E MIAOB-6FE367F6B1 MIAOB-FED1304FC9 MIAOB-8735E83EC0 MIAOB-2626CD9664 如果有人体验后愿意反馈一下： - 哪些网页识别效果比较好 - 哪些成语没有识别出来 - 哪些功能比较有用 - 哪些地方使用起来不顺手 我会继续改进。

projects.title: Show HN: Like LeetCode, but multi-file and multi-step
projects.author: mrtie
projects.summary: On LeetCode you write one function, it passes, and you're done. Most AI labs such as Anthropic and OpenAI, as well as some big tech companies such as Meta, Snowflake and Databricks, don't stop in one function and instead ask multi-step questions that are closer to real-world problems. Say you're building a key-value store. Step 1 is get, set, delete, count. Once your tests pass, Step 2 unlocks: expiring keys. Then nested transactions. Then atomic batches. I built this because I couldn't find a good place to practice for multi-step, multi-file questions. The questions are based on ones people have reported from those loops. Check it out at https://loopprep.dev . There are 24 questions, 3 free, and no signup to try them. Happy to answer questions.

projects.title: Show HN: Pinocchio: Harness for Verifiable Work
projects.author: lazaruslong
projects.summary: Hey HN, we've been trying to solve LLM Hallucinations. So we built Pinocchio. Pinocchio is a research preview for AI outputs with provenance and verification built in. Give it a task and source material. For numerics, the values used in the computation are carried directly from the source rather than regenerated by the model across reasoning steps. Pinocchio records the computations and derivations applied to them, and a deterministic verifier can replay and check the resulting computation. The output retains a connection to: • the exact source inputs used • the operations performed on them • the intermediate and final results they produced • the checks those results passed Every output points back to its sources. You can trace it backwards through its derivation and sources. Really looking forward to what you guys think about this. P.S. we're limiting to one run at a time. Other than there are no other restrictions. It does take a while though, so I'd let it be and check back in a while.

projects.title: Show HN: I made a tiny MoE/Engram viz tool
projects.author: softwarewright
projects.summary: As part of a ML study group I've been building tools to experiment with ML concepts. I use AI Coding agents to develop software, mostly cloud-based but I keep trying local LLMs on 12G, 16G, and 24G VRAM GPUs. Freetoken has made it possible to run larger MoE models on smaller GPUs. This inspired me to use my ML tools to build a tiny MoE model from scratch so I can experiment with different agent optimizations and things like Engram, recursive models, hierarchical modeles, KV Cache compression etc. My link above shows results of building different tiny models, one dense, the rest MoE variants. There is a lot of code and tooling behind this. Goals: - build tiny MoE models that run in a browser to give interactive help (today I use deterministic matchers to respond to user queries; still researching how to improve this with better trained MoE models). - build tiny MoE models that run on small ARM and RISC-V development boards, possibly using NPUs (using no_std Rust). My tools are an alternative to Python, ML libraries, Jupyter notebooks, and Google Colab. My approach is a REPL and/or AOT Compilable array-programming DSL written in Rust. This language has ML concepts as first class language elements and built in visualization primitives. It runs in a browser via WASM. It runs at the CLI on both Apple and Linux (supporting Apple GPU and NVIDIA GPU libraries, Ollama-based REPL context-senstive help). It is extensible via dyamic plug-in Rust libraries. I have created many demo repos showing how to use this ML array language for ML tasks, learning Math concepts, general purpose programming. You can build desktop apps, (Ruby on Rails inspired) CRUD apps. So you can create ML experiments and visualize data in the browser or on the desktop. It also supports Emacs org-mode for literate programming. This tiny MOE Microscope is just my latest demo of this approach. I hope it helps someone learn more about MoE experts, routing, Engram, etc. It helped me learn more.

projects.title: Show HN: Notula for Google Meet
projects.author: anetrebskii
projects.summary: Hi HN. I built this because quite often all these tools that transcribe save it somewhere in their own storage, so you have to pay for it. And if not the payment, another bigger issue is that this storage is in another place, where I need to copy from. And of course I don't want to pay for storage that I'm not going to use, because I have my own place for such documents and transcriptions. Once I met a nice tool that just records the transcription and does nothing else. You copy the transcription and paste it wherever you want. But at some point it stopped working properly. Then there's another issue. I used it a lot, but it requires you to keep the transcription open all the time, and it takes up space on the Google Meet page. For instance, if someone shares their screen, it's smaller because of the transcription, which I only needed for the extension. So I wanted to make it better, and that's why I built it. On transcription it does the same, it just saves locally, but it doesn't keep the transcription open at all, so you get the full space of your browser in Google Meet. You can copy the transcription to your clipboard and paste it in your place, or download the MD file, whatever you want. And just recently I updated it and made it save to my git repository automatically. You pick the repository, you pick the folder, and it is saved there. That part goes via Notula, my desktop editor, but I don't want to force on you some extra tools that I don't need myself, so everything else works without it. It used to be called MeetScribe, and two identifiers inside it still say meetscribe. They have to. They are how two content scripts find each other, and renaming them breaks every Meet tab that is open at the moment the update lands. I would love it if you would kick the tires and let me know what you think of it. Happy meetings! --- Website: https://notula.org/meet/ Chrome Web Store: https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/notula-for-google-m... GitHub: https://github.com/anetrebskii/meetscribe

projects.title: Show HN: STXT, indentation-based format with schemas and no escape characters
projects.author: mombiela
projects.summary: STXT is a human-first text format for documents: it has very few rules and is designed around simplicity and readability. The goal is a language that people write naturally, and machines parse securely and reliably. Compared with XML, you keep namespaces and schemas, but without closing tags or escape characters. There is no entity expansion or external resource references either. Compared with YAML or TOML, every value is text (no Norway problem), a text block is literal, and schemas are STXT documents too. The combination of STXT and Markdown allows validated and structured documents, with the expressiveness of Markdown. To explain it, I've created the main portal https://stxt.dev , made with STXT itself (add .stxt to any URL to see the source). In the portal you can find all the specifications, the tutorial, VSCode extension, a CLI, parsers in Java, TypeScript, Python, and a playground: https://play.stxt.dev . All available in https://github.com/stxt-lang/ . An example in STXT (extra indentation for HN): Book (com.example.library): Title: Modern Software Architecture Authors: Author: Keyla Brown Author: Joan Costa ISBN: 978-84-123456-7-4 Published: 2026-08-25 Summary >> This book offers a practical view of patterns and best practices for designing distributed, scalable systems. And the template with the structure and cardinality: Template (@stxt.template): com.example.library Structure >> Book: Title: (1) Authors: (1) Author: (+) ISBN: (1) Published: (1) DATE Summary: (?) TEXT Why STXT? I created STXT in the spring of 2013, as a language that preserves the most used of XML, while being able to be written by non-technical people. The first version was finished, different from the current one, but I never announced it. In 2014 my daughter was born; my priorities changed. Time passed, other languages were created, and we arrived at 2025. In those years I didn't find another format with the same balance of characteristics that STXT has, and I decided that was the time to resume the project. Since then, I've been revising the language, using it for personal projects, and I consider it usable and stable. I'd love to have your feedback, impressions and comments.

projects.title: Show HN: Godot and Rust based multiplexer (terminal panes and more)
projects.author: 1nv1n
projects.summary: I wanted to share my side-project: gPTY. Started off as an idea to combine Godot and Rust in a project (two stacks I wanted to use more to learn more). The base inspiration was tmux - simply allow spawning multiple PTYs and then let the user grid/tile them how they see fit. But since we have the Godot game engine at our disposal, we can do some more interesting things, like add an FPS counter, and then subsequently also let people set their preferred FPS (the idea being the potential lower power draw if someone's running it on a laptop on battery power vs someone running it on a desktop with high/native FPS). In its current state, with me using Oh-my-Pi a lot, it's evolving into a terminal workspace that can be used for orchestrating autonomous AI agents by way of dogfooding (or you know, just run herdr inside of gPTY - it's the better orchestrator and just good software - I found it after starting this project, and now I'm finding myself using it a lot). Also, we're not limited to just terminals. Since we have Godot, we have basically a 2D (and potentially a 3D) canvas to play with. We can already full-screen the app for "zen" mode, no taskbar, no distractions. TUI die-hards can have their media or other apps entirely in terminal panes. There has been some ground-work on getting Markdowns displayed properly done and I want to work on some kind of Wiki framework for local knowledge-management next, then create more types of panes (think native audio/video on a media pane, that sits alongside your terminal pane), and some simple 2D games (like snake) to prototype. More details are on the ROADMAP. What's not easy (and probably won't happen) is a browser. Having done a couple of (small) projects using Electron already, the temptation to ditch Godot/Rust (learning curve) did come up (and also the ecosystem, the ease with which I could pull components and use web technologies - development velocity would definitely be higher there). But on the flipside, given all of the available LLM and AI support that we are privileged to have today, I figured the velocity should be comparable depending on how much I leaned on those. And lean I did. Godot/Rust seemed the better call to me and my intent anyway - going with the 'it's not just the end but the journey that matters' philosophy. So yes, there has been heavy use of LLMs & AI to generate a lot of the code. But I do review and steer actively, not relying solely on vibes, and there's a few bits here & there that have been human authored. There are definitely a lot of polish and QoL items that need to land to make the end user experience better, but in the meantime, let me know your thoughts and/or concerns! Repository: https://github.com/godot-pty/gpty Docs/Blog: https://godot-pty.github.io/gpty/

projects.title: Show HN: Caffenol, a darkroom simulation photo editing toy
projects.author: vintagevibe
projects.summary: Caffenol is a darkroom toy, built on film development and darkroom craft. You load a photo and develop it into a negative in a simulated tank. Then you print that negative under a timed enlarger exposure. You shape the light by hand with cut cards that you wave over the paper. Under the hood, it's a WebGPU-powered film and paper sim, with chaos from each run producing a unique, organic result. It's built to encourage experimentation and there are few guardrails. I built this because darkroom printing made me fall in love with editing photography in a way Lightroom or Capture One couldn't. But it's expensive, uses a lot of resources, and isn't accessible. So, Caffenol brings the process and makes a few opinionated turns so it's fun and enjoyable. Ultimately, I hope it helps people make cool art. I'm tuning the film and paper sims with B&W processes now, with color coming shortly (read: when the color process can be made as fun as B&W is). No signups and everything is stored locally. If you find yourself wanting to learn more about how to bend and break it, the manual might help: https://caffenol.app/manual/ Hope it can make a print worth saving.

projects.title: Show HN: A Modern C++ course with videos and interactive GitHub homeworks
projects.author: soinus
projects.summary: Hi HN. Over the last couple of years in my free time, I’ve been designing and recording a complete modern C++ course. I wanted to share it here in case people still care about things like this in this brave new age of AI. The course is absolutely free and consists of: A GitHub org that holds written lectures and all other resources and tools: https://github.com/cpp-for-yourself The accompanying YouTube course (43 videos to date): https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLwhKb0RIaIS1sJkejUmWj... My main goal was to design a course that leaves nobody behind. Every single lecture relies strictly on concepts explained in previous ones. We start from an absolute beginner baseline (a simple "hello world", variables, functions, and control flow), move through manual command-line compilation, libraries, CMake, and unit testing with Google Test, and then push into deeper territory: memory management, smart pointers, the mechanics of move semantics, dynamic vs. static polymorphism, and parallelism. While there is always more to know with C++, I believe that the course, as it stands now, covers the majority of the things a C++ engineer should know to succeed at an average work place. At least when talking about C++17 (and C++20 to a degree). I chose C++17 as the baseline partially because I started the course some years ago and partially to also cover the needs of people in automotive, military, and medical branches as those are usually lagging behind in their allowed standard version. Throughout the course, I aimed to use simple yet realistic examples, both in the lectures and for the interactive projects. I also deliberately favored simplified intuitive explanations over rigorous pedantic language, which I found makes modern C++ far less intimidating to learn, while hopefully not encouraging bad habits. A few practical details on how it’s built: - The Lectures: The material lives in Markdown files containing full lecture scripts and code snippets. All code is checked validated to build and every animation is typescript code written with Motion Canvas. The repo with code is here: https://github.com/cpp-for-yourself/lectures-and-homeworks - The Homeworks: The course includes practical projects. You create your own homework repository from a provided template, work on the assignments, and open PRs there. A custom CI setup automatically builds your code, runs your tests, injects my own test suite to validate your solution, and reports the results back in a dashboard directly on your PR. See the template repo here: https://github.com/cpp-for-yourself/homeworks Because this project spanned a couple of years, things changed along the way. For example, I lost some hair and gained glasses. But jokes aside, my recording setup and teaching style evolved a lot. The earliest videos feel quite different from the later ones. I stand by the technical content of the early lectures but vastly prefer the later style of delivery, geared a bit more towards entertainment while staying factual. If you want to sample this newer style, start from the second half of the course, somewhere after the move semantics lecture. Please tell me if you think such an endeavor is useful and if the format suits your liking. I take HN community criticism very seriously and will definitely account for it in any future videos that I record (or rerecord) for this course. Thank you for your time! P.S. I went back and forth on whether to use "Show HN" here, but ultimately decided to use it because the course is completely original, built from scratch, and structured around an interactive GitHub codebase akin to an open-source technical book. Happy to adjust if the moderators feel otherwise.

projects.title: Show HN: Fashionguessr – A Daily Fashion Trivia Game
projects.author: WhosTiki
projects.summary: Hello! I created Fashionguessr, a daily fashion trivia game. Inspired by other daily trivia games like Timeguessr, Connections, and Wordle, Fashionguessr is my attempt at the same thing for people curious about fashion. The game is broken up into three parts: Runway Frames - Users have to guess and identify a fashion show, its brand, its season, and its designer based on a single random frame from the show. Users can use a variety of hints, each more expensive than the last, to reveal more information about the show to help them guess correctly. Trivia - Multiple-choice and short-answer questions to test their knowledge about fashion, the lore, the people, the processes, the history, and everything in between. Sketch - Users get a few moments to look at a fashion item and then are tasked with drawing it from memory. All of these contribute to a score you can see at the end on the last page, which sums everything up. Each section includes explanations, summaries, and sources, so users can get as much insight as possible for every question. There are new questions every 24 hours, and users can go back and play games from days past. I built it to help people learn more about fashion in a fun, low-stakes environment. Learning about fashion can be overwhelming, and I think Fashionguessr can present and package fashion education in a way that's more palatable. Would love feedback on the presentation, UI, accessibility, ease of use, and anything else that comes to mind.

projects.title: Show HN: I built an AI Agent that sell itself
projects.author: akhtaaar
projects.summary: Quick bit of context: SendRoq is a LinkedIn automation tool. Before the AI era (pre-2021), I ran a marketing agency. Back then, client acquisition on LinkedIn was all manual. Once AI agents started becoming a thing, I built one for my agency's internal use, never intended to sell it. It worked really well for us. A few colleagues and partners kept pushing me to turn it into a SaaS. I said no, we were already profitable running the agency, why complicate things. Then a few weeks later, I was on an onboarding call with a new client, and he asked, "How did you guys know I was looking for marketing help?" I told him straight up: we have an AI agent that analyzes LinkedIn profiles and picks up on signals. If someone comments, engages, or posts anything hinting they're looking for marketing, it flags it and reaches out. He got interested immediately and wanted to buy the agent for his own sales team, was ready to pay well for it. I told him it wasn't public, not for sale. He pushed back: "So make it a SaaS." That conversation is basically what got the ball rolling. A few months later we actually started building it out. The hardest part, unsurprisingly, was getting our first users. Our GTM was pretty meta: we used our own tool to book meetings with potential customers and sell them directly.

projects.title: Show HN: You can't read every ToS, but the clanker can
projects.author: PAndreew
projects.summary: Termsinator is a public registry of LLM-performed analyses of public legal documents like ToSs, Privacy policies, Cookie policies, etc. The goal of this project is to help people better understand how their data will be used, and what potential pitfalls they need to avoid. Why? You know that feeling of enlightenment and sense of control after you've red dozens of pages of legal mumbo-jumbo before subscribing to a service? Yeah, neither do I (well, maybe some of you do and mad respect for that). I've been encountering more and more reports on how corporations abuse ToSs, Privacy policies and the like to push data collection and retention to really orwellian depths - and thus openly declaring that they deem their (paying!) userbase sheepishly stupid. I don't know the solution to this problem, but Termsinator is a stab in this direction. What? The idea is very simple: - let the clanker read and analyse the legal stuff - collect the results in a common place so everyone can access it - help people make better informed choices - rinse repeat On a high level this is being implemented in the following way: - scrape public facing legal docs - forward it to an LLM, which will analyse it, and evaluate the content based on several metrics (see the docs) - store the results along with some metadata - present these on the website - and also provide people a browser extension that can pull these results automatically (if they exist of course) I'd like to honestly declare (not that it's not obvious) that this is a PoC and it's an LLM generated codebase (Python + Go + Astro written mainly by Sol in/with? the Pi agent). At the moment I manually trigger the analyses and since I'm poor I'm using a dirt cheap and thus not super bright Qwen model to do the reading. My goal with this Show HN is to gauge if such a project even makes sense. If you find it promising I encourage you to try it, contribute to it or just spread the word. :) PS.: The logo was carefully crafted by my totally human hands and not part of a new "draw me an angry robot-like SVG face" benchmark.

Looking forward to receiving some feedback or learning more about how people access/work with their agents on the go. Also if you encounter any bugs please report them on Github, if a feature is missing you'd really want to see, open a discussion. projects.title: Show HN: Locksmith: Store Maven Secrets in the macOS Keychain (Or a Unix Socket)
projects.author: exabrial
projects.summary: Hello HN, In the age of LLMs sucking in random secrets, sandbox escapes, and RCE orbital bombardment, I thought it'd be a good idea to create a Maven Extension that defers to the MacOS keychain for resolving secrets. In general, it's a good idea to not have any secrets (passwords, tokens, etc) stored in plaintext files. Also, this allows your machines to be FIPS-140 complaint, if thats a thing for your job. Locksmith is a Maven Core Extension that defers to the MacOS Keychain. The entry format in settings.xml looks like: `{[type=locksmith]nexus.superbiz.example.com/username}` This was a fun project and I used the Project Panama FFM with jextract for the first time. The FFM is a great iteration on JNI (which still has it's place) and was pretty much brainless to use. Setup is quick and easy and I tried to make the readme as friendly as possible. As an aside, I've also architected the core Library indecently from the Maven bits, so if you do need to read from the MacOS keychain in a project, you could pull the core Library in without dragging in Maven. Being 2026, of course Claude was used to assist in the creation of the project, however Locksmith is not vibecoded top-to-bottom. I personally loathe AI slop. I use LLMs as a tool, not a crutch. Enjoy!

projects.title: Show HN: Pragma Twice – A dystopian sci-fi themed programming game
projects.author: umvi
projects.summary: Hey HN, I'm Bryan. I released Pragma Twice earlier this week in anticipation for Steam's "Programming Fest". Pragma Twice is a programming puzzle game in the same vein as Untrusted ( https://untrustedgame.com/ ). You have to write real JavaScript code to incrementally improve your playable character's "kernel" over the course of the game. Beating levels autonomously (without keyboard inputs) reveals a competitive time/code golf aspect to the game. I started developing Pragma Twice over 4 years ago after playing Untrusted and loving it. It took so long to develop because I'm not a full time game developer... between my actual job, my kids, and my own self-motivation, it's taken a lot longer than I originally hoped to get this game shipped! It's definitely what you might call a passion project. Anyway, I plan to keep iterating on it, so give it a spin and let me know what you think! A few technical details/challenges: - The game was originally written in vanilla JavaScript, but I later converted it to TypeScript (which had an astonishing ROI) - Uses PixiJS for the graphics and a custom game engine built around Web Workers + SharedArrayBuffer for sandboxing and guarding against things like infinite loops - The web version is hosted on GitHub Pages, which was challenging because of the SharedArrayBuffer requirement (I use https://github.com/gzuidhof/coi-serviceworker to work around this) - The linux/windows versions use Electron - Uses CodeMirror for in-game editor/console - Levels built with LDtk - Automated game testing with Puppeteer Steam: https://store.steampowered.com/app/3528840/Pragma_Twice/ Dev Notes: https://www.bryanpg.com/games/pragma_twice

projects.title: Show HN: Give your AI agent on-screen guides that show users where to click
projects.author: pancomplex
projects.summary: Hey HN. I'm Christian, one of the founders of Frigade (YC W23). I've noticed that a lot of in-app AI agents struggle to actually understand the products they exist in. For instance, let's say a user asks an agent how to do something in a given SaaS product. In an ideal case, maybe that agent replies saying it has a tool to do the task and just automates that work entirely for the user. That's a great outcome. But often that's not the case. Maybe there is no tool call for that exact task, or maybe the user's question is best solved by a specific UI workflow or interface. In these cases, many agents tend to fall back on basic RAG on their help center, or sometimes even searching the internet for an understanding of their own product. This can be a very slow process and most of the time help center articles are outdated as products evolve faster than them today. Even worse, no one likes reading a long list of bullets and mapping that back to a UI. My tool (Assist API) solves this gap with a single tool call defined like this: const frigade_guide_tool = { description: 'Call this tool to answer product questions or guide the user through a task.', parameters: { query: { type: 'string', description: 'What the user is asking or wants to do', }, }, run: ({ query }) => frigade.assist({ query }), } Here's a demo I recorded on how to set it up with the Vercel AI SDK: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9WQ0UbLjC6I When called, the tool will do the following: 1) Gather context on what the user is seeing on screen, their permissions, feature flags, and more. Then one of the following: 2a) If solvable: Generate an on screen guide for how to fix a given problem 2b) If conceptual: Return text describing to the parent agent how to solve the problem 2c) Reject (i.e. unable to help) How does the tool know what to do? The tool learns a given application UI by using a browser-based agent. You provide a test account to your software (i.e. staging og preview), and a browser agent logs in and works its way through the entire product. It then builds its own map of how the application works which can the be queried about any product-related question or how to get from A to B in the UI. It also writes its own documentation from this map. The agent re-runs on a schedule or can be triggered through CI/CD. Docs and more details: https://frigade.com/assist-api

projects.title: Show HN: Intro-level book about quantum computing theory/hardware/applications
projects.author: msolomentsev
projects.summary: Hi HN - If you're anything like me, you've seen the occasional quantum computing posts here and skimmed through them, hoping that the comments would explain the significance (or lack thereof) of the results in question. I got to the point where I just wanted to read a proper book about the field, so that I could understand what quantum computing 'is' at a high level (I'm technical, with an EE PhD, but not a physics or CS guy). Unfortunately, I found that there wasn't really a text that fit my needs. There are books that explain the math/CS theory at an appropriate level (I recommend Scott Aaronson's Quantum Computing Since Democritus and Thomas Wong's Introduction to Classical and Quantum Computing), but nothing that deals with the hardware or the applications (both of which I am very interested in). So I did a lot of self-education and paper-reading, and wrote the book I wanted to read. It's called Quantum Computing for the Confused, and it's available online (and in pdf/epub) completely free. It's fairly short (40k words) and meant to be accessible to audiences with a bit of technical literacy. I'll also note that it is 100% human generated! :) The book has four sections, each looking at a different aspect of quantum computing: its theory; how these systems are implemented in real hardware; what quantum computers may be used for; and what the industry looks like today. I think this work fills an important niche in layman-oriented writing about the field, which I think does not do a good job making itself intelligible to outsiders. If you're interested, you can find it here: https://quantumcomputingfortheconfused.com/ Happy to discuss and chat further. Cheers!

The biggest change is the addon architecture: the core stays small, with no third-party dependencies, and you add what you need (JWT, OpenID Connect, automatic Let’s Encrypt certificates, Swagger, Razor, dependency injection, or logging integrations). I wanted a server I could understand and modify easily, while keeping extra functionality in separate packages. projects.title: Show HN: LazyReader – Read ebooks and stream audiobooks directly from your cloud
projects.author: ekaftnuocca10
projects.summary: I built LazyReader because I was tired of re-importing the same ebook library whenever I switched devices or reading apps. Most reading apps copy your books into their own storage. LazyReader connects directly to your existing cloud storage, so your books stay where they already are. It supports Dropbox, OneDrive, and Nextcloud. You can browse your library and read EPUBs directly from the cloud, and it now also supports streaming audiobooks directly from cloud storage. So if you have a 1GB M4B audiobook, you don't need to download the entire file to your phone before listening. Since the original version, LazyReader has grown into a much more complete reading app: - EPUB and audiobook support - Library and reading-progress synchronization - Collections and sorting - EPUB and audiobook edition linking - Offline reading and listening - Offline dictionary - Word and phrase search - Notes and highlighting - Text-to-speech - Theming - Multiple cover-enrichment options - Book metadata editing - QR-code book sharing - Interactive/choice-driven EPUB support The interactive EPUB support is probably one of the more unusual parts. EPUBs can contain much more structure than a typical linear ebook, so LazyReader can handle branching and choice-driven books as well as conventional EPUBs. The main idea is still the same as when I started it: your books are your files, and your cloud storage is your storage. LazyReader doesn't require you to import everything into another proprietary library. "LazyReader on Google Play: https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.lindocode.... Requires an account so your library, reading progress, and cloud-storage connections can be synchronized across devices. I'd be interested in hearing what people think, especially about the cloud-based approach and audiobook streaming. Happy to answer questions about the implementation or anything else.

projects.title: Show HN: Decode, encode, listen, and speak to learn a language
projects.author: Lublub
projects.summary: Hey HN. I love learning languages and I have tried several language learning apps over the last few years, but I didn’t like any of them because they were either expensive ($20-$50/month) or weren’t very effective. I was using Duolingo, for example, because it was free, but it was slow and ineffective. Even after having ~150 day streak, I still couldn’t say much in Spanish. I was either passively listening to the language, learning vocabulary without context, or learning sentences that weren’t realistic. So I set out to build my own. I have tried different approaches and techniques over the last 1.5 years for learning a language, and finally found something that works well. This web app uses a 4-step system of decoding, encoding, listening, and speaking. 1. Decoding: You are given a sentence in your target language (e.g., French) and have to unscramble the English words to figure out what it means. 2. Encoding: The exact opposite of step one—translating the active thoughts from English back into your target language. 3. Listening: You listen to the native audio of the sentence and type out the English translation. 4. Speaking: You hit the record button and actually practice speaking the sentence out loud from day one. I have been using this app for a while now, and it has been helping me learn French far more effectively than my previous approach. It gets me speaking the language from day one, I learn vocabulary and grammar through context, and I learn phrases and sentences that are practical and realistic. I am excited to finally launch it and get it into the hands of other language learners. I would love to hear any feedback you have on the method or the app itself! I’m currently running a free private beta. If you want to test it out and help me improve it, you can test the 4 steps in the website demo or sign up for free here: https://www.4tospeak.com Caleb

projects.title: Show HN: I was tired to check my mums WhatsApp last online, to see if she is ok
projects.author: janrakete
projects.summary: Ever since my father passed away, my mother has been living alone in our family home. She’s now over 70 years old. I live in another city, and so does my sister. Of course, we call her regularly, but at the same time, she doesn’t want to feel like she’s being watched. She’s still too “young” for that. So our best way to check on her is to see when she was last online on WhatsApp. But in the long run, that’s too imprecise and, above all, too much of a hassle. A while back, I set up a few smart home features in the house. But they're mostly things like turning down the thermostats when a window is open or using a motion sensor to turn on the lights. Then I had the following idea: Why not use this data to identify behavioral patterns? In other words, if a door isn’t opened the way it usually is, that could mean something. My mom now has a FitBit Air, too, which provides data. That would be great as well. But to do that, all the data with its different connection types (Zigbee, Bluetooth, external APIs) needs to be consolidated. The fact that they’re all from different manufacturers doesn’t make things any easier. That’s how my open source project "Healthcore" came to be. Healthcore is an open software and hardware architecture for (healthcare) devices. "Healthcare" is in parentheses because, in theory and practice, standard smart home components can also be used, but in the long run, I’d like to include things like blood glucose monitors. Think of Healthcore as similar to OpenHAB or Home Assistant, but with a greater focus on intelligent data analysis and actions tailored to healthcare. Incoming data is standardized. For each device, there is converter. Healthcore uses various anomaly detection methods across the collected data to trigger alerts. These alerts can then be used to define actions in scenarios (e.g., if blood sugar is unusually low at night, turn on the lights and send a push notification). Reports can also be generated from the data using a locally hosted LLM. Healthcore also supports LoRa P2P for transmitting data over long distances. Healthcore is currently headless. However, anyone can quickly build their own interface using the Swagger file. The Healthcore is meant to be the foundation for my startup, bulp.io. With bulp.io, I’ll build or license my own hardware, which will, of course, be 110% compatible with the Healthcore. My primary target audience is my mom, followed by other people living alone, and then nursing homes. What do you think? Is this a good idea? Feel free to check out the repository on GitHub and give me some feedback.

projects.summary: 1. 项目地址 项目仓库： 线上体验： 视频演示： 2. 项目亮点 本项目是目前 GitHub 上较少见的覆盖 “用户画像—职业规划—岗位采集—人岗匹配—数据分析” 完整流程的纯 Python 项目。 对用户进行画像分析时，在考虑用户简历的基础上，还考虑了用户的性格特点。 各阶段分析结果，均可查、可复制、可下载，具有较高的可观察性和可控性。 3. 项目展示 3.1 工作喵 🐱 上传简历 + 回答 15 个偏好问题，生成用户画像、职业报告、岗位检索词，也可以直接和 AI 聊求职。 3.2 爬虫喵 🕷️ 使用 DrissionPage 自动采集招聘岗位信息，检索词和筛选条件都可以自己设置。 3.3 分析喵 📊 岗位少的话，直接交给 LLM 分析；岗位多的话，先用 RAG 筛出相关性最高的 50 个，再让 LLM 做详细的人岗匹配。 3.4 工具喵 🛠️ 合并岗位、查看 TOP 岗位、分析单/全岗位、数据可视化，都可以在这里实现。 4. 注意事项 本项目仅用于学习、研究与技术交流，请勿用于任何违法或违规用途。 线上 Demo 暂不支持爬虫功能，建议根据视频教程进行本地部署。 AI 生成的分析结果仅供参考，请结合实际情况进行判断。

github.description: TK试题题库是一款面向教师个人和教育机构的 Windows 桌面题库与组卷软件，以本地离线使用为核心，数据默认保存在本机。支持富文本与数学公式编辑、Word/Excel 批量导入导出、学科/章节/标签分类检索、重复题检测、手动选题与随机抽题、试卷分页排版及打印，并提供题库统计、回收站、备份恢复和数据目录迁移功能。基于 Tauri 2、Vue 3、TypeScript、Rust 和 SQLite 构建，结合 Tiptap 与 canvas-editor 实现录题和试卷编辑，Word 文档处理无需依赖 Microsoft Office。源码包含桌面客户端、官网、测试及授权工具，采用 MIT 许可证，欢迎教师和开发者共同改进。

projects.summary: BCTK（TK试题题库）是我维护的 Windows 桌面项目，用于把零散教学题目整理到本地 SQLite 题库，再按章节、标签选题并编排试卷。支持 Word / Excel 导入导出、公式编辑和备份恢复。使用 Tauri 2、Vue 3 与 Rust 开发，源码采用 MIT 许可；当前程序仍保留试用和基础模式限制。开发者可以参考其中的桌面文件处理、题库管理及分页编辑实现。 亮点 将题目整理、分类检索、选题组卷、排版和历史保存串成一个教学工作流程，本地使用无需云账号或单独部署数据库服务器。 Word 文件在本机通过 Rust 模块读取与生成，无需调用 Microsoft Office、WPS Office 或 LibreOffice；支持范围和复杂文档限制在 README 中列明。 录题使用 Tiptap 与 KaTeX，试卷排版使用 canvas-editor，可以参考富文本内容在编辑器、分页稿和文档输出间的处理方式。 提供中英文 README、三张真实界面截图、构建步骤、测试及架构说明，以及附 SHA-256 校验文件的 Windows 安装包。 使用范围说明： 安装包保留 15 天专业版试用和 15 天宽限期，之后基础模式每卷最多 10 题，关闭批量导入、文档导出和打印。MIT 源码许可不会自动改变程序的默认授权行为。独立云服务端未包含在仓库中；安装包没有 Windows Authenticode 签名，缺少 WebView2 时安装需要联网下载运行环境。详情见 v0.1.83 Release。 截图或演示视频 以下为浏览器演示模式的实际截图，使用内置示例题。文档导入导出、备份等文件操作需在桌面版使用。

projects.summary: 自荐一个免费开源小工具：CSV Local / CSV 中文乱码本地修复，由本账号使用 Codex 辅助制作。 在线使用： 源代码（MIT）： 离线 ZIP： 它针对的是 UTF-8 CSV 在 Excel 双击打开乱码、旧系统 GBK / Big5 导出需要转换，以及程序导入要求无 BOM 的情形。所有文件读取和转换都在浏览器内进行，不上传文件、不加载第三方脚本，没有账号和运行时依赖。 选择文件 → 手选或检测编码 → 核对前 8 行预览 → 导出 UTF-8（可带 BOM）。导出只转换编码，保留原有分隔符、引号和换行。自动检测仅覆盖有效 UTF-8 和带 BOM 的 UTF-16，其他编码需手选，避免假装能可靠猜出所有编码。 使用边界也写在页面上：不支持 XLSX，不恢复已经写成问号的文字，不解决 Excel 长数字截断，不清理 CSV 公式；请保留原文件，仅处理可信 CSV。最大文件 5 MiB。8 项核心测试覆盖 GBK、UTF-16、BOM 和引号内换行等情况。 附有中文乱码排查指南，引用微软官方导入建议。所有功能和离线版免费；项目页附自愿赞助入口，不设付费解锁。

projects.title: 【开源自荐】PolyJump：可配置 三维 棋盘游戏 AI 研究环境
projects.author: SanZiNEO

github.name: SanZiNEO/poly-jump
github.description: A configurable 3D jump-chess framework with A/B geometries, multi-player rule switches, and RL/self-play training support.

projects.summary: 我是 PolyJump 的开发者，自荐一个开源项目：PolyJump。 它不是又一个 2D 跳棋游戏，而是一个“不同空间路径模型 + 可配置规则 + 多人博弈”的 3D 棋盘 AI 研究环境。 传统棋类大多建立在二维平面上；即使一些项目标着“3D”，也大多只是把多个二维面组装成一个三维外形，展开后仍然是一张平面。PolyJump 不只是在视觉上做 3D，而是把棋盘本身的空间路径结构作为可配置变量——不同的空间路径模型、2/3/4/6/8 人局、多种移动方向、中国跳棋 / 西洋跳棋 / 混合规则，让 AI 面对的不再是固定环境，而是多智能体、需要空间规划和搜索的博弈任务。 在线试玩 👉 效果 功能 7 种空间路径模型：A / B / C / D + A-ext / B-ext / C-ext 移动方向：6 / 8 / 12 / 14 / 18 / 20 / 26，根据模型自动匹配或自定义 玩家数：2 / 3 / 4 / 6 / 8 移动规则：普通移动、跳跃、连跳、两格跳、自由停、强制跳到底 游戏模式：中国跳棋、西洋跳棋（吃子）、混合模式 积分制：连跳、吃子、进目标区、胜利奖励，可配置开关 3D 前端：HTML + Three.js，渲染、合法路径高亮、AI 自动对弈、回放、中英文切换 后端：Python + FastAPI，HTTP API 和纯后端 GameEnv AI 研究：airesearch/ 基准评测，支持批量对局、指标统计、时间戳归档 一个初步发现 同一个 MCTS 搜索算法放在 A / B / C / D 四种几何模型上，路径选择会系统性不同： A / D：MCTS 更容易找到更短路径 B / C：MCTS 更容易走长连跳，detour 更高 这说明几何结构本身就会影响 AI 的空间规划策略。 完整报告：docs/11-cross-geometry-discovery.md AI / 研究接口 外部程序可以通过 Python 接口直接驱动游戏： python from backend.game.config import PolyJumpConfig from backend.game.env import GameEnv config = PolyJumpConfig(geometry="B", bradius=6, players=2) env = GameEnv(config) obs = env.reset() while not obs.done: actions = obs.legalactions 接入你的 AI：MCTS / RL / LLM Agent 等 action = actions[0] obs = env.executeaction(action) airesearch/ 提供不依赖前端的批量评测，目前包含： random / manhattan / euclidean / chebyshev / graphbfs MCTS 搜索 baseline PettingZoo AEC 包装（fullaction / primitive） 输出胜率、action/step 指标、路径距离、目标区进出指标，结果归档到 airesearch/runs/<时间戳>/。 快速开始 bash pip install -r requirements.txt python run.py

projects.title: Show HN: The Analyst (A data science analytics simulator)
projects.author: Stuart_Jones
projects.summary: In data science and analytics, it is often somewhat difficult for new analysts to get a grasp of the field before actually starting at a real job. During education, the task is often contained and clean: "Here's churn.csv, choose a model and report the metrics." But on the job it is often much less clear, much more expansive, and beckons a much more holistic judgment: "The Director is meeting the Legislature at noon Monday, this needs to be on my desk by 4 on Friday. Here's a handful of tables that might be helpful, but there are many idiosyncrasies in them. Also, we aren't entirely sure what about the Director's meeting is supported by the data, but I'm sure you can figure it out. Good luck." I built The Analyst as a flight simulator of sorts for the field. You get dropped in as a new analyst in a fictional company with millions of rows of data and dozens of tables and asked to develop real products exercising real judgment. It's all free and open-source and requires no accounts, signups, or personal info, and all of it exists in the browser. You perform SQL, Python, and the summary work inside the browser, and there's export options for GitHub portfolios, to share socially, or to give to your instructor for evaluation. And yes, there's an Instructor Desk for those teachers, giving them guidance and direction. Importantly, there are no answer keys anywhere: the website gives concepts and ideas you should pick up on, but the deep judgment evaluation is left for another human. I'm definitely excited about it, and while there are a lot of places online that encompass parts of the vision here, almost all require payment and are closed-source. I truly hope this site proves useful for many people! I'd love any feedback you all have. Thanks much.

projects.title: 【开源自荐】Super：用 Rust 写的 API-First 进程编排器 —— Supervisor / PM2 的现代替代品
projects.author: hzbd

github.name: schiplat/super
github.description: The API-First, Lightweight Process Orchestrator for the Edge.

projects.summary: 背景介绍 每台服务器上，总有一批需要“长期活着”的进程：自建网关、队列 Worker、边缘采集脚本、或者本地运行的模型推理服务。 管好这些进程，大家通常会选择经典的 Supervisor 或 PM2： 但 PM2 拖家带口带着庞大的 Node.js 运行时，在精简 VPS 或边缘设备上显得格外沉重； Supervisor 的配置和体验还停留在 ini / CLI 时代，缺乏原生的现代 HTTP API，CI/CD 和 Agent 很难通过代码灵活操控； 至于 systemd，它虽强大但强依赖 root 权限，不跨平台，且动态管理进程门槛高；而 Docker Compose 有时又显得杀鸡用牛刀，很多人并不想为了两个常驻脚本去承受构建镜像的额外开销。 为了兼顾“极致轻量”与“可编程性”，我们用 Rust 编写了 Super：一个无额外运行时依赖的 API-First 轻量进程编排器。 架构设计：极简清晰的双二进制 Super 采用了经典的 Daemon-Client（守护进程 + 客户端） 架构，打包发布为两个独立的纯静态二进制文件： superd（后台引擎 / Daemon）： 核心守护进程，通常作为开机自启系统服务静默运行。它负责进程生命周期托管、健康检测、崩溃重启、日志汇聚与安全沙箱，并对外暴露统一规范的 REST API & WebSocket。 super（命令行客户端 / CLI）： 提供给开发者操作的终端工具。super 本身不直接拉起进程，它只是 superd 的一个官方 HTTP API 客户端。 这意味着：你在 CLI 里能做的一切，CI 流水线、自动运维脚本、或者外部 Agent 都可以无缝直接调用 superd 的 API 实现。 核心特性 Rust 纯静态编译，零运行时依赖：无 Python、Node 等环境依赖，只有 superd 和 super 两个体积精巧的二进制文件，极简容器、精简 VPS、边缘盒子直接开箱即用。 API-First（进程即可编程资源）： 单行命令托管：super add --name demo --autostart python3 -m http.server 8080； 声明式栈管理：支持通过 TOML 声明服务依赖链、健康检查与环境变量，一条 super apply 一键收敛整套服务栈； 原生标准接口：彻底告别解析 CLI 终端文本输出的时代，所有状态查询与管理均走标准 HTTP/WS。 崩溃自愈与稳健守护：异常退出自动拉起、退出码判断、启动时延防护、优雅停机（SIGTERM ➔ 超时 SIGKILL），该有的守护逻辑一个不少。 平滑无损发布（事务式更新）：服务版本更新内置事务保障：“备份 ➔ 校验 ➔ 切换 ➔ 失败自动回滚”，告别手工替换文件重启赌命的裸奔操作。 可观测性与事件账本（Audit Ledger）：实时日志流（WebSocket）、历史日志检索；内置事件账本，记录服务状态变更的完整因果链，出事能复盘，不靠盲猜。 默认安全：superd 默认仅监听本地 Loopback 地址（可按需配置监听外网并启用鉴权）；敏感环境变量在 API 与 CLI 输出中自动脱敏打码。 一条命令自动注册系统服务：安装脚本在校验 SHA-256 后，会自动将 superd 注册为各平台的系统自启服务（Linux systemd / macOS launchd / FreeBSD rc.d），开机自启无需手写 unit。 快速上手 1. 一键脚本安装（推荐） 通过官方自动化脚本完成安装（自动校验 SHA-256 并注册 superd 为系统开机自启服务，非 root 用户可能需要 projects.title: Show HN: Gigantic Research, Friend
projects.author: KnoxProtocol
projects.summary: https://giganticresearch.com Yo whats up everyone? So let me drop right into it and not waste your time if you are reading this. I instantly grew a dislike for arXiv when I spent days writing up a research paper and then came to find out I need an endorsement to post at all. No pun intended, I should have done research but it was a slap in the face, especially since that same paper was accepted to ICTAI 2026 by someone who did the research for fun, 0 financial backing, 0 institutional backing, 0 affiliation. Research shouldn't be gated like that. Research is research and I can't imagine the amount of good, ground breaking research from everyday people that never sees the light of day because of this. Sure there is Zenodo, but you still have enough options to tell your lifes story which certainly effects viewership. And they have their own gates mechanism which is communities, want to post to a specific community where your audience is present? hold on there buster, needs to be reviewed before you can post. So i thought to myself, this is dumb, research is research and there should be a place for just that. and that might exist but I wanted to make my own version of it. So I did, giganticresearch.com. Its aim isn't to compete, its aim is to aggregate research from anyone who has something they want to share, no preferential treatment, the only research on display is the most recently uploaded research. You want your research shown? upload more! you want one of my 7 tiered badges that mean absolutely nothing but a cool little something next to your name that shows how much you've contributed? then make an account! and here is the wonderful part, you dont need to make an account to upload, anonymous is the default. I store 0 data on where it came from. The only thing an account does is ties you to the research, gets you a badge that means nothing really, and the ability to show you what you've uploaded and what you have favorited. The option to delete your account is there as well, and all the research you uploaded if you choose that option. Anon uploads stay uploaded. I wouldn't have a way to track an anon upload anyway because I store no data but the upload itself and the sha 256 tied to that research. There are two hard no go research topics that I will not allow to be uploaded, and you can read about on the About page. Other than that, push it, thats the point. I want us to have a research depot where you can find just about anything. Big or small. And it doesnt need to be YOUR research, it can be any research you want to share, on pretty much any topic you want to share. Also I implemented a forum, where anon is the default too, but feel free to use your account if you want there as well. The account is also just there to give you a handle to go by. No data is stored on that either in terms of identifying you. The anon part isn't there to be evasive per se, its also there because in this day and age, it seems privacy is less and less a thing, so if I can provide that in some way, then I will. I've been trying to promote this all day and I haven't had one person upload anything. It is just some of my research that I used to seed the site a little bit and thats it. So if any of this sounds interesting to anyone reading it and if you have any research you would like to share, if you could take a few mins and upload to my website I'd appreciate that and I thank you in advance my friend. I made the site as frictionless as possible, time is the only currency that matters in this world, the most valuable currency and the one currency we can not acquire more of, and I value your time so I made sure to make the process take up as little of it as possible. Again, I thank you for reading this even if you dont upload anything, and I double thank you if you do, either way, you get a thank you from me.

projects.summary: 我是 Minta 的开发者，自荐一个开源项目：Minta ()——面向 AI 智能体的上下文质量层。 一句话：它不只是又一款 AI 记忆库，而是给记忆做生命周期管理的质量层——检测"哪条记忆已经过期、哪两条在互相打架、哪件事 AI 根本没做过却声称做过"。 记忆工具教不会 AI 记忆,几乎所有的记忆工具都在解决"怎么记住"。这是我跟"记不住"这件事死磕三个月，逼出来的结论。你叫它"别动 tests 目录"：它学了。可它不知道的是，可能这条规则已经过时了，因为你上个月早就改主意了；又或者，它把三个月前试错的旧方案，当成宝贝推荐给你。而且上午刚讲过的话，下午新会话又问你一遍。 所以，存得住 ≠ 信得过。Minta的做法： 过期检测：定期扫描，把过时的记忆标记、归档——不靠 LLM 自己"觉得"过时了 冲突表面化：两条记忆矛盾时，不把两个都塞回 prompt，而是摊开给你决定 纠正闭环：你纠正 AI → 进收件箱 → 你确认 → 变成规则。一次纠正，长期生效 证据分级：按证据强度设门控，"没做过实验的事，不允许声称做过" 60 秒本地跑起来，无云、免费： bash git clone && cd minta python mintacli.py start # MCP 工具，Claude Code / Codex / Cursor 直接接 3 分钟接入（Windows 实测一键）： github.com/xinchen03/minta → Download ZIP → 解压 双击 startminta.bat（自动装依赖，弹网页+菜单） 菜单选编辑器：Claude Code / Codex / DeepSeek Harness / Cursor 了解更多：awesome-dsh-plugin.com/p/xinchen03/minta--dsh-plugin/ DSH 用户安装：dsh plugin --profile web add @xxinchen/dsh-plugin Context Health——记忆生命周期仪表盘 () 核心引擎和记忆中枢 UI 全部开源；研究驾驶舱等高级面板通过 API Key 激活。项目还很新——但"记忆会过期、会打架、会自说自话"这个问题，大概每个把重要事情交给 AI 的人都会撞上，也许值得一看。

projects.summary: 【开源自荐】Resume Builder：让 AI agent 像聊天一样陪你写简历 我是 Resume Builder 的开发者，自荐一个开源项目：Resume Builder。 传统 AI 简历工具，通常是“填表 → AI 优化 → 导出”。用户输入被局限在表单里，AI 也只能在平台规则内帮你改，改完就结束了，讨论、口径、红线都留不下来。 Resume Builder 换了一种方式：你下载项目，在豆包、Codex、DSH 这类 AI agent 里加载 AGENTS.md，然后直接聊天，AI 会像一位简历顾问一样，陪你一块一块改。 和在线 AI 简历工具不同，这不是 SaaS，而是本地开源项目：用户下载后在自己的 AI agent 里加载，数据是本地 YAML，并带有 reference 记忆区和 HTML 中间产物。 特点： 内容全部是本地 YAML，不需要懂 YAML，AI 负责写 每个 YAML 末尾有 reference 记忆区：用户原话、口径、红线、待确认事项都记在这里，构建时自动截断，不会进入最终简历 一个 YAML 一个 YAML 讨论修改，不一次性生成整份简历 中间产物是 HTML，AI 可以直接读 HTML/CSS：用户说“超页了”“不要红色”，AI 能直接定位并修改 一份标准简历可以复制成多个岗位 JD 定制版本 一键导出 HTML / PDF / 长图 / 分页 PNG 开源、本地、无账号，数据在自己手里 快速体验： bash git clone cd resume-builder python -m pip install -r requirements.txt python make.py build --person demo 打开 output/demo-/demo-.html 就能看到效果。 项目还很新，我更想分享的不是“又一个简历生成器”，而是“简历不应该靠填表，应该靠聊天”这个想法。

projects.summary: PhyAgentOS 是一个面向物理智能体（Physical Agent）的开源 Harness 框架，由中山大学 HCP 实验室、鹏城国家实验室具身智能研究所与 X-Era Lab 联合研发。 项目希望解决 AI Agent 从数字世界走向物理世界之后面临的核心问题：如何让不同机器人快速接入，让算法与 Skill 自由组合复用，并让 Agent 在真实环境中完成执行、验证、反思与持续进化。 PhyAgentOS 将 Agent 的高层认知决策与底层物理执行解耦，把机器人、算法和 Skill 统一抽象为可调用的 Tool。Agent 只需要判断“下一步做什么”，而无需直接适配具体机器人 SDK、控制器或仿真环境。 目前主要包含几个核心能力： 异构机器人快速接入：机器人动作统一通过 Forge Gateway / Tool API 执行，上层 Agent 不直接依赖具体硬件 SDK，同一套 Agent 与 Skill 可以迁移到不同机器人本体。 Skill 自由组合与复用：将感知、规划、操作、导航等基础能力封装成 Tool / Skill，并进一步组合成长程任务，避免每个机器人、每个 Demo 都重新开发一套流程。 执行结束 ≠ 任务完成：PhyAgentOS 将 Execution、Evidence 与 Verdict 分开处理。机器人完成动作后，系统会结合动作前后的图像与状态证据，判断用户目标是否真正达成。 失败后自动重新规划：如果 Verifier 判断任务没有完成，Agent 会基于当前环境状态生成新的 PlanRevision，继续完成任务，而不是简单重复之前的动作。 在交互中持续进化：经过验证的任务过程可以沉淀为可复用 Skill 与作用域内的 Lesson，让 Agent 将真实执行中的成功经验和失败反馈带入后续任务，形成 执行 → 验证 → 反思 → 改进 的闭环。 目前 PhyAgentOS v1.0.0 已于 8.31 正式发布，采用 MIT License，支持 Agent、Tools、Skills、MCP、Memory、任务验证、失败恢复与经验进化等能力，项目已获得 2k+ GitHub Stars。我们也正在持续接入更多机器人本体、算法工具和真实任务，希望逐步建立一套面向 Physical Agent 的开放基础设施：让 AI Agent 不只会调用数字世界的工具，也能够真正走进并理解物理世界。

projects.title: 【开源自荐】patent-compose-skill: 一个从项目文件到专利布局的全流程工作流
projects.author: yizchu

github.name: yizchu/patent-compose-skill
github.description: AI驱动的专利撰写工作流，自动化完成项目分析、查新检索、专利组合生成与优化、交底书和流程图撰写。

projects.summary: 在技术创新落地的过程中，专利申请始终是很多团队的卡点：研发人员懂技术却不懂专利撰写逻辑，IP 从业者想高效挖掘创新点却受限于项目材料的零散，企业要做专利布局却缺乏系统化的评估方法，要么保护范围过窄容易被规避，要么过宽缺乏创新高度。 patent-compose-skill是一款AI驱动专利撰写工具，通过引入权利要求树拆解技术方案，辅助专利布局，并自动多源检索，经六轮攻防对抗优化组合方案，适用于交底书撰写、专利申请材料撰写、创业公司布局及批量挖掘创新点。 工作流最核心的设计是「权利要求树」体系。不同于传统的文字交底，工具会自动遍历源代码、架构文档、设计稿等项目文件，将技术方案拆解为层次清晰的树状结构：每个节点对应一项技术特征，节点间的包含关系直接匹配权利要求书的撰写逻辑，同时支持标注特殊设计点，让独立权利要求与从属权利要求的布局一目了然。 在此基础上，工具实现了专利组合的智能化优化。它支持多源并行查新，同步对接 CNKI、FreePatentsOnline 等数据库，自动生成检索词并输出结构化的三性评估报告，精准定位区别技术特征。随后通过六轮攻防对抗模拟 —— 从审查员的新颖性检验，到竞争对手的规避路径测试，再到等效侵权验证和最终合规审计 —— 逐层打磨权利要求的保护范围，最终输出平衡了保护宽度与稳定性的专利组合方案。 这款工具既可以帮助研发人员快速输出规范的技术交底书，也能辅助创业公司完成初步专利布局，还能为大型企业的批量创新点挖掘提效。需要说明的是，它目前定位为专业辅助工具，最终申请文件建议由专利代理人审核把关。 亮点 1. 权利要求树结构化转译，打通技术到专利的语言壁垒 自动解析源码、技术文档、设计稿等多类项目文件，将零散的技术方案拆解为层级清晰的树状特征结构，节点间的包含关系直接匹配权利要求书的撰写逻辑，替代传统人工梳理，解决了技术人员不懂如何从自己做的项目中提炼创新点、交底书表述不规范的痛点。 2. 多源联合智能查新，输出结构化三性评估报告 自动基于技术特征生成中英文多组检索词，并行检索 CNKI、全球专利数据库，还可补充非专利文献检索；自动逐一比对技术特征，明确独有创新点，输出包含新颖性、创造性、实用性评估的专业查新报告，同时给出授权风险点与应对建议。 3. 六轮攻防对抗机制，迭代优化专利保护范围 突破 “一次性出初稿” 的传统模式，模拟审查员、竞争对手法务、专利律师等多角色视角，通过新颖性筛查、规避路径测试、等效侵权验证等六轮攻防迭代，动态调整权利要求的宽窄与表述，平衡 “保护范围” 与 “授权稳定性”，同时支持多专利的组合布局规划。

projects.title: Show HN: I audited my SEC pipeline, found 82.7% of split adjustments were wrong
projects.author: Loris_jk
projects.summary: Hello HN! I built a pipeline which fetches SEC EDGAR 10k and 10qs for more than 600 companies, maps xbrl-tags onto around 35 financial concepts and computes growth- , fundamental- and valuation-multiples (prices provided by yfinance). This project originated bc I wanted clean, non-third-party financial data in order to judge a trading thesis of mine. I could not find any app providing such data (for free), let alone being open source. Turns out there are no data providers because xbrl of 10ks and 10qs SUCKS(!!!!). It is messy, unregulated and devastated. Its the wild west of finance. A project like this was 5 years ago not possible, at least not with less than ~1000 people. Thats because of the nature of xbrl-tags. Since they are unregulated, a certain xbrl-tag could fit perfectly for a certain company, while providing nothing, only a partial amount, or complete garbage for another company. You would have to iterate through every financial statement ever relesed by a company, searching every tag possbile, comparing, once found, a tag and constantly checking, once more companies are added to the obserable universe, if the tag also produces meaningfull data for those new companies. As I said, unmanagable task. Except for LLMs. I used Anthropics Claude Fable 5 mostly, giving strict, non-regression focused tag research tasks, constantly letting it iterate through the entire ticker universe, searching and comparing tags. And it worked. It took me around 3 weeks just to produce wrong data, manually searching for a ticker universe of 3 (AAPL, MSFT, NVDA). Now this pipeline produces correct, cleaned data (more on that later) for more than 600 companies. That was just the main problem tho. Notable problems taht also had to be fixed: -companies tagging everything as fy ull year; -cash flow being filed cumulative; -q4 is never filed; -a quarter isnt always the same length; tag changing by a company; -STOCK SPLITS (god i hate them); -companies reporting wrong (a few 0s more for example); Still got a lot of work to do, UI and UX are...rudimentary. Appreciate any feedback/critics. Thanks for taking your time reading this. repo link: https://github.com/lorisjk/stock_valuator

projects.title: 做了个"每天待办"小工具：可以自定义每天要做的事，可以跳转 APP
projects.author: defiabell
projects.summary: 做了一个自己的 TODO 工具，这种工具很多，但是没有自己做的灵活可控。有啥点子都可以自己去实现。 简单说，这就是一个网站，在手机上可以将其放到桌面，使用上和 APP 没区别。 这个工具的特点是可以自定义跳转其他 APP ，例如我的待办是运动，我可以跳转 Bilibili 对应的视频。 在线用（公开实例，免费，不用部署，中英文）： https://yixi-app.pages.dev/today 截图： https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Defiabell/yixi/main/docs/images/today-paper.png 仓库（ MIT ）： https://github.com/Defiabell/yixi == 它长什么样 == 一屏上只放几件正在做的事。默认三件，可以改，我劝你别改多。因为每天最重要的事就那一两件。 每件事下面挂几条每天都要做的小事。比如「学英语」下面是「听读三遍」和「背 20 个词」，「健身」下面是「跟练 20 分钟」。这些不是一次性待办，是每天都要勾一遍的；勾完最后一条，这件事今天就自动算做了，卡片右上角的圆圈亮起来。 每张卡下面一排七个点，是过去七天。回看页能看到本周每件事做了几天、勾了几次。就这些。没有积分，没有连续打卡天数，没有提醒。 每条小事都能绑一个跳转。填的不是「 B 站」，是 bilibili://video/BV 号，按下去直接落在那个视频上；微信读书是某一本书，不背单词是某个词书，Keep 是某个课程，能给出 URL scheme 的 App 都行，https 链接也能填。 填的时候有个「试跳」按钮，App 真开了才算配好；不知道填什么可以按 App 名字查候选。填错了不会坏，只是跳到首页而已。 == 一些实在的 == 它是个网页，加到 iPhone 主屏幕就是一个不用安装的小 App 。勾选是即时反馈的，请求在后台走，断网了会退回整页刷新，不会出现半截状态。 存了什么：你写的目标和子任务、每天勾了哪几条。就这些。不放心公开实例就自己部署一份，Cloudflare Worker 加 D1 ，免费额度，十五分钟，代码同一份。 == 预判几个问题 == 「和 Things / 滴答清单比呢」——不比。那些是清单，能放一百条；这个故意只放几件，放不下的事就是今天不该想的事。 「为什么不做成 App 」网页加系统自带的能力够用，不用装、不用审核、不用订阅，改起来也快。 「安卓能用吗」页面是普通网页，安卓能开能勾；跳转靠 URL scheme ，安卓那边我没试过，欢迎试了告诉我。 「子任务每天都一样，不会腻吗」会。所以它没有连续天数、没有奖励，腻了就改，改完的那一刻它又只是一页纸。 欢迎试用

projects.title: Show HN: TimerVana a Local-first scheduler for real world routines
projects.author: granto
projects.summary: Hi HN, I’m the creator of TimerVana. It's not just "another timer app". The engineering analogy is a lightweight task scheduler for things people do in the real world. A normal timer models one countdown. TimerVana models a small dependency graph in JSON: some steps run sequentially, others run in parallel, and everything can converge on a target finish time. You can also combine multiple timers (e.g., combine a timer with all the steps to cook a steak + a timer for roasting vegetables). I originally built it because I often set multiple timers and alarms when cooking and got tired of repeatedly juggling separate alarms to get a main dish and several sides ready together. The same model also works for workouts, study sessions, morning routines, and other repeatable processes. The iPhone app is local-first by design [0]. You can create, save, and run timers entirely on your phone without an account or cloud sharing. If you want the networked features, the companion website lets you browse and download timers, upload your own, and share them with other people. Everything available today is free. I may eventually add optional AI-assisted timer creation as a paid feature, but I haven’t settled on the business model or pricing. I'm more doing this to solve my own problem and hope it will help others as well. I’m interested in whether the underlying abstraction makes sense: does a sequence of dependent and parallel timed steps help you? I’d also appreciate feedback on the balance I took between the completely local experience and the optional sharing layer (I was partially inspired by the old iOS Workflow App, which was acquired by Apple and is now called Shortcuts). Of course, any other feedback very much appreciated. [0]: https://apps.apple.com/us/app/timervana-share-complex-timers...

projects.title: Show HN: DanTerm – a fast macOS terminal emulator (compare with Ghostty, iTerm2)
projects.author: hombre_fatal
projects.summary: danterm started out as a small AppKit wrapper around libghostty so I could get vertical tabs. Repo: https://github.com/danneu/danterm About 3-4 weeks ago, I decided to replace libghostty with my own Swift terminal engine implementation, and the whole project is just Swift with no third-party deps -- only Apple's swift-collection for a Deque impl. I started with a naive correctness implementation that passed third-party tests, and then I incremented to the optimized release of today with things like a packed byte arena for scrollback that grows on demand. The result is that it's an 8 MB application that sits at 52 MB with 10 empty tabs open and grows to just 250 MB when those tabs are filled with 10k lines each. (kitty: 240 -> 790 MB, ghostty 1.3: 780 -> 1400 MB). It also has the best pty throughput as measured by kitty's `kitten __benchmark__ --render`. Perhaps most interestingly is that this project is my latest experiment in how to use rigor to automate high-quality software with LLMs. I use things like ADRs, a docs/research/ system, a review/revise cycle on plans, and multi-pass workflows to pay back debt and find code improvement opportunities. For example: https://github.com/danneu/danterm/blob/749942ffa1198f520c8b7... This project has put yet more writing on the wall, for me, that most software -- and then all software -- can be fully automated with just a human "taste-maker". It has some cute features like: - A `danterm <command>` CLI - A replayable pty flight recorder (`danterm tape`) - Usual fare like tabs, panes, themes, search, and a recovery system so that you can close danterm, reopen it, and it reads its prev state from disk. Even has a gimmicky todo system (per pane and per tab). - A semantic model powered by shell/agent integrations where you notify danterm things like "command started (vim foo.sh)" and "agent waiting (claude code)". This seemed a lot more reasonable than trying to cleverly determine the state of the session from the pty stream. - A companion iPhone app that lets me control danterm remotely over Tailscale - A reusable Swift terminal engine that compiles on Linux (for fun, I started a gtk4 frontend) Anyways, I hope it's interesting. It was a lot of work and it's my daily driver terminal.

projects.title: Show HN: Votito helps you decide what to build next with confidence
projects.author: gojkoa
projects.summary: Hey HN, We're finally launching Votito, after about a year of development, as it's now (almost) polished enough for other people to use. I'd love your feedback! AI tools make software faster to write, so the constraint is no longer building things. It is knowing which things deserve to be built. Votito aims to be a "product decision platform" to help figure that out. Having previously built two relatively successful SaaS products, we've spent a ton of time figuring out what users need, collecting feedback and trying to turn signals from the user community into actionable ideas, using a bunch of disconnected tools and half-baked scripts. We've consolidated those internal tools and processes into an online idea management system, combining user feedback with product research, so product teams can engage their users easily. Votito is not trying to compete with task management tools like Jira and Linear, but to work in the area before the backlog, in the "weak commitment" zone where unstructured proposals need to mature to become implementable ideas. Throw random stakeholder demands, user suggestions and feature requests into Votito and let them marinate until they become something useful, if they ever do. Votito will help you spot the gems that deserve your attention. It will also stop garbage from going into your actual task tracking tools, and prevent people from being overwhelmed with managing bad ideas. While the product is naturally oriented towards PMs, we're betting on the trend that teams are becoming smaller with AI support, and that people inside delivery teams will need to take on most traditional product responsibilities in the future. The Wall Street Journal recently reported on the trend of "pods" of 3-4 people augmented with AI agents taking on the tasks that previously needed much larger groups. When teams have 10-15 people, companies can justify assigning a dedicated product person. But with 3-4 people per pod, this is just not feasible. GitHub's research from December 2025 found that developers will increasingly need to think at the level of "understanding user needs". One of our goals is to put proven product methods and tools into the hands of people who are not traditional product managers, making it easy to discover and apply the right tools and, crucially, to understand the results. Here are 5 ways Votito can help you decide what to build next: - Collect evidence with ideas to help you prove that things are worth building. Evidence can be as simple as a list of interested customers, external documents such as market research, or something as complex as the result of an A/B test. - Score ideas automatically based on impact, effort and evidence. We provide two popular confidence models out of the box to help you get started. - Engage users or stakeholders to vote on ideas for additional confidence signals. - Keep the community engaged. Let people propose new ideas directly in Votito, comment and vote on other people's proposals. Publishing a roadmap of ideas you've accepted into development, and a changelog of features you delivered recently. - Conduct deep research with proven product management surveys. Feature requests are pointers that something is interesting, but they are rarely complete information, or even the best solutions for the problem. Votito allows you to easily run online surveys with people who voted on a proposal. We provide a collection of ready-made templates for major product management research tasks. You could, of course, set up a similar survey on another platform, but the difference is that we'll help you interpret the data, showing the best ways to score domain-specific surveys and evaluate statistical significance. The free version includes pretty much everything you need to run all the things mentioned above, with data retention of up to six months.
